subject: physics
title: Direct and alternating current
key_idea: In direct current (d.c.) charge flows in one direction only. In alternating current (a.c.) the movement of charge keeps changing direction. UK mains electricity is a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz and about 230 V.

blocks.text: A current can flow one way, or it can keep changing direction. The two types are named by what the charge does.

items.meaning: The movement of charge in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply direct current.
The movement of charge changes direction, over and over.

items: The same difference applies to potential difference. A direct potential difference is always in the same direction.
An alternating potential difference continuously changes direction.
A phone charger changes the 230 V a.c. from the mains to a smaller d.c. output.

diagram.alt: A direct potential difference stays constant in one direction. An alternating potential difference swings positive and negative over time.

items: d.c.: charge moves in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply d.c.
a.c.: the movement of charge keeps changing direction.
Say current, potential difference or charge flow, not just electricity.

blocks.text: The electricity supplied to homes in the UK is a.c. Two values describe it.

items: Frequency: **50 Hz**. The unit is the hertz.

diagram.alt: Sort each statement into direct current or alternating current.

checks.q: Describe the difference between direct current and alternating current.
checks.a: In direct current the charge flows in one direction only. In alternating current the movement of charge changes direction.

checks.q: Give the frequency and the potential difference of the UK mains supply.
State the type of current supplied by a battery.

exam_phrases: direct potential difference is always in the same direction

mistakes.wrong: The mains supply has a frequency of 230 Hz and a potential difference of 50 V.
mistakes.right: Frequency 50 Hz, potential difference 230 V. When the question asks for frequency first, answer in that order.

mistakes.wrong: The unit of frequency is written as 50 on its own.
mistakes.right: The unit is a separate mark. Write 50 Hz or 50 hertz.

worked_example.question:
Mains electricity is an a.c. supply.

Explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference.
answer_points: Direct potential difference is always in the same direction.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each type. Direct current or alternating current is allowed in place of potential difference.

mistakes.wrong: Electricity supplied to homes has a frequency of 230 Hz.
mistakes.right: The frequency of the mains is 50 Hz. 230 is the potential difference, in volts.

worked_example.question: Describe the difference between direct current (d.c.) and alternating current (a.c.) in electrical circuits.
answer_points: d.c.: the current is in one direction only.
worked_example.tip: One way and both ways are accepted for the directions.

mistakes.wrong: d.c. is when electricity flows in one direction.
mistakes.right: The word electricity is ignored. Say the current, voltage or charge flow has one direction.
d.c. has one direction or polarity. It can be only positive or only negative. a.c. alternates between positive and negative.

worked_example.question:
The high voltages across the power lines are reduced to 230 V a.c. for use in the home.

A phone charger changes the 230 V a.c. to a 5 V d.c.

Explain the difference between d.c. and a.c.
answer_points: d.c.: the current (or voltage or charge flow) has one direction or polarity.
a.c.: the current (or voltage or charge flow) continually changes direction or polarity.
worked_example.tip: d.c. only positive or only negative is allowed, and a.c. alternates between positive and negative.
